video_title: How FTX Taught a Crypto Lawyer Not to Make Crypto Her Identity: DEX in the City
gist: Final episode of Dex in the City, a panel of three women crypto lawyers (ex-SEC, ex-DOJ, Chainlink GC) offering career advice, keeping perspective through volatility, and recounting the FTX collapse's emotional toll. Light on market signal; most useful for the institutional-adoption anecdote and crypto-legal convergence points.

insights.claim: Crypto legal work now spans securities law, the CFTC, EU rules and money-movement regimes at once, because teams build chains and products that combine spot trading, perpetuals, tokens in other countries and prediction markets.
insights.speaker: Jesse/V panel lawyer (guest)
insights.so_what: Product convergence in crypto raises demand for cross-regime legal and compliance generalists and raises the compliance burden for multi-product platforms.
insights.quote: it's usually like chains for everything or products for everything

insights.claim: A guest advises against treating 'getting into crypto' as a career category, arguing that if the vision of crypto as a layer under everything materializes, 'crypto' stops being a distinct sector.
insights.speaker: Guest lawyer
insights.so_what: Talent and employer framing is shifting from crypto-native to domain-plus-crypto, a sign of mainstreaming.
insights.quote: I don't think you should ever consider getting into crypto as getting into crypto

insights.claim: Guests recommend that non-engineers in crypto learn how products work, including who has control, how assets move, how smart contracts operate and where the risks sit, because credibility depends on technical substance.
insights.speaker: V (ex-SEC enforcement attorney)
insights.so_what: Control and asset-flow literacy is the practical diligence lens for assessing crypto protocol risk.

themes.theme: Industry maturity and mainstream institutional adoption

insights.claim: A former DOJ crypto prosecutor says that around 2016-2017 she had to beg the FBI to take cases involving terrorists using Bitcoin and nobody in government cared, whereas now institutions that once dismissed crypto, including the FBI and banks, are curious or leaning in.
insights.speaker: Jesse (ex-DOJ, now Rivet Capital)
insights.so_what: Shows how far institutional and government attention has shifted, a lagging indicator of adoption.
insights.quote: real institutions that laughed us all out, whether it be the FBI or a bank or whatever, they are now the ones that are curious about it or at least leaning in

insights.claim: A guest argues crypto's core technology has changed less than AI's: it still rests on the blockchain and tokenization concept from Bitcoin, extended by Ethereum and smart contracts, so progress has come from persistent adoption pushes rather than rapid technical churn.
insights.speaker: Jesse
insights.so_what: Crypto adoption is framed as a distribution and policy story, not a technology-race story.

insights.claim: The hosts say crypto's early conformist, us-against-the-world culture was a survival response when it was unclear the industry would survive, and that an immature industry benefits from open debate and dissent.
insights.speaker: V
insights.so_what: Groupthink risk in crypto discourse may leave narratives mispriced; private agreement with dissenters is often greater than public noise suggests.
insights.quote: crypto can have uh a very sort of conformist culture

themes.theme: FTX shock and separating identity from industry

insights.claim: A guest recounts that days after FTX collapsed she became too emotional to continue a previously scheduled Senate office meeting, saying FTX felt like a personal betrayal because she had tied her identity to defending the industry.
insights.speaker: V
insights.so_what: FTX's reputational damage reached even policy advocates emotionally, which helps explain how hard the 2022 collapse hit the lobbying push for clear rules.

insights.claim: The guest's lesson is to separate the potential of the technology and the reasons for believing in it from the actions of bad actors in the industry, and to keep building what should exist.
insights.speaker: V
insights.so_what: Resilience through cycles depends on thesis-based, not identity-based, conviction.

insights.claim: Panelists say 2022-2023 was a very rough period but that this is not the last down cycle, and recommend staying connected to people outside crypto while also keeping a peer group of crypto general counsels as support.
insights.speaker: KK Catherine (Chainlink Labs)
insights.so_what: Durable crypto operators treat volatility as cyclical and build external support, which is relevant to team retention in downturns.
insights.quote: this is not the last down cycle that we're going to experience

themes.theme: Women and outsiders in a male-dominated industry

insights.claim: Guests say the situation for women in crypto has not improved this year despite the effort invested.
insights.speaker: Jesse
insights.so_what: Diversity gaps persist in crypto leadership and policy voices, which affects who shapes the legislation process.
insights.quote: I don't think the situation for women in crypto has gotten any better this year

insights.claim: A guest says that the industry needs to understand how to talk to all constituencies, citing a recent bill that did not pass as evidence that crypto is not a homogeneous group.
insights.speaker: Jesse
insights.so_what: Internal industry splits are cited as a factor in a legislative setback, a risk for market-structure bills.

insights.claim: A crypto lawyer says her skills in reasoning about crypto legal issues transfer to understanding the technical issues of AI, and that she spent free time building with AI and sees value in combining crypto and AI knowledge.
insights.speaker: Jesse
insights.so_what: Crypto-legal talent is migrating toward AI and crypto-AI fusion work.

insights.claim: Panelists note they mostly look to X for AI ideas these days and recommend podcasts such as How I AI and Women in Tech to follow AI tooling.
insights.speaker: Jesse
insights.so_what: Attention among crypto professionals is rotating partly toward AI.

insights.claim: Panelists disagree on X: one says crypto professionals are at a huge disadvantage without it because news breaks there first, another says to rely on primary sources such as releases and statutes rather than social media for regulatory information.
insights.speaker: KK Catherine
insights.so_what: Regulatory news flow in crypto is real-time on X, but primary documents are the reliable source for legal interpretation.
insights.quote: if you're in crypto, you actually have to be on Twitter
